clue.text: King in trouble with son's relatives

indicators.note: in places the king inside the word for trouble, enclosed by its letters

parts.note: to trouble someone is to bother them
R is short for Rex, Latin for king
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A monarch in difficulties because of his son's family.
explanation.walkthrough: BROTHERS: the king sits inside BOTHER, then S for son follows; the 's of the surface is read as 'has' and joins the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Brothers are male siblings, a kind of family member or relation.

clue.text: Research scientist's book no longer available, I note

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
a dish that is off the menu is no longer available
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A scientist's book has gone out of print, someone observes.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as 'has', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Boffin is British slang for a scientist or technical expert, especially one doing research.

clue.text: Nothing dispirited European recently

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
feeling flat means feeling low, dispirited
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European who has lately become utterly downcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Of late is an adverbial phrase meaning lately, in the recent past.

clue.text: Former Conservative leader initially healthy and fit

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter
an ague is a fit of fever and shivering

explanation.surface: A past Tory leader who was hale and fit at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' poses as an adjective meaning healthy; it is the noun for a bout of illness. William Hague led Britain's Conservative Party from 1997 to 2001.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hague is a British politician who was leader of the Conservative Party, opposition leader 1997-2001.

clue.text: Man possibly prohibits sunglasses

parts.note: Ray is a man's name, one possible man
to prohibit is to ban

explanation.surface: A man perhaps refusing to allow shades to be worn.
explanation.definitionFit: Ray-Bans are a well-known brand of sunglasses, so the brand stands for the eyewear.

clue.text: Cease heartless language

indicators.note: a heartless word has lost its heart, the central letter

parts.note: the tongue spoken in Finland

explanation.surface: An instruction to stop using unkind words.
explanation.walkthrough: FINNISH has seven letters; taking out its central N leaves FINISH.
explanation.definitionFit: To finish something is to stop or end it, a plain synonym of cease.

clue.text: Wrong criminal or nicer court?

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so these letters are bent out of shape

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Ct is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Asking whether a court is mistaken, crooked or kinder.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation CT joins the anagram fodder, and the whole set of nine letters is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Incorrect means not right or accurate, which is a direct synonym of wrong.

clue.text: Wobbly old seat I detached

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady and shifting, so the letters move around

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to having pulled apart a shaky old chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detached' reads as the speaker's action on the seat; it is the adjective meaning separated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something isolated is set apart and alone, which is what detached means.

clue.text: His Excellency is upset with art gallery's delay

parts.note: HE is the abbreviation for His Excellency, the title of an ambassador

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and in a down answer that turns the word upside down

parts.note: taken as written
the Tate is a group of famous British art galleries

explanation.surface: An ambassador is annoyed by the gallery's slow progress.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the London art gallery; the 's reads as 'is' in a definition-at-end clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To hesitate is to pause before acting, so it means to delay.

clue.text: Loudly, everyone teases scapegoats

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
everyone is all of them
to guy someone is to mock or tease them

explanation.surface: Something said noisily: the whole crowd mocks those who took the blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loudly' looks like a sound-alike signal but is simply F from music notation. To guy is an old-fashioned verb for ridicule.
explanation.definitionFit: Fall guys are people made to take the blame for others, which is what scapegoats are.

clue.text: Vexed after a type of crossword clue?

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the word for vexed is placed behind the article

parts.note: taken as written
vexed means annoyed, cross

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed after a certain kind of crossword clue defeated them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vexed after a' tells us CROSS comes after A. The question mark flags the self-referential definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword clues are grouped as either across or down, so an across clue is one category of them.

clue.text: Miss start of school and sleep

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the first letter
kip is British slang for sleep

explanation.surface: A pupil misses the first lesson to have a nap.
explanation.definitionFit: To skip something is to miss it out deliberately, such as skipping a class.

clue.text: Clueless, hopeless thinker carrying plug around

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the word for plug runs right to left
to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within the other
something hopeless is a mess, so the letters of the next word are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a plug is a piece of publicity, an advert or ad

explanation.surface: A desperate philosopher lugging an electrical plug about, with no idea what's going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plug' suggests an electrical fitting; here it is the slang for a free advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the dark is an idiom for being uninformed, having no clue.

clue.text: Slate roof half scratched by a stone

indicators.note: with half scratched out only the front two letters of that word survive

parts.note: taken as written; only half is kept
taken as written
st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A slate on a roof gets scraped by a falling rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slate' looks like a roofing material in this setting, but it is the British verb for harsh criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: To slate and to roast both mean to criticise someone severely; this is the verb sense, not the tile.

clue.text: In the US, shoot rodents

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an exclamation of annoyance; American speakers say 'shoot!' for the same feeling

explanation.surface: Americans going out to shoot vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' reads as firing a gun at the rodents; it is actually the mild American curse.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection 'Rats!' expresses frustration just as 'Shoot!' does, and the plural noun names the animals.

clue.text: American soldiers in welcome consensus

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American

indicators.note: in puts the soldiers inside the word for welcome, surrounded by it

parts.note: to welcome someone is to greet them
soldiers are men in the ranks

explanation.surface: US troops being given a warm reception everyone agrees on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American soldiers' suggests GIs, but the two words act separately: A and MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: An agreement is a shared view or accord reached by everyone, which is a consensus.

clue.text: Porter oddly opening hamper

indicators.note: oddly means taking the letters in odd-numbered positions only

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters
a vent is an opening or outlet

explanation.surface: A railway porter is strangely opening a picnic basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' looks like a basket the porter carries, but it is the verb meaning obstruct.
explanation.definitionFit: To hamper something is to hinder or block it, and to prevent is to stop it happening.

clue.text: Imagines ancient Scots crossing river

indicators.note: crossing means spanning over something, so one piece straddles the other

parts.note: the Picts were a people of ancient Scotland
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Pictures an old Scottish tribe fording a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a river of North Yorkshire, a favourite crossword river.
explanation.definitionFit: To picture something is to form a mental image of it, so pictures means imagines.

clue.text: Allude to present attitude

parts.note: someone present is in, at home
a stance is an attitude or position

explanation.surface: Hinting at someone's current point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as an adjective on attitude; it gives IN, as in 'is anyone in?'
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to instance means to cite as an example, which is a way of referring to something.

clue.text: Took no notice of developed region west of Germany

indicators.note: in an across answer west means to the left, so this piece comes first
something developed has been worked into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: Someone overlooked a built-up area on Germany's western border.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignored is the past tense of ignore, meaning paid no attention to something.

clue.text: Some clod or knucklehead

indicators.note: some means part of, so the answer is a run of letters inside the words that follow

parts.note: found across the end of clod, the word or, and the start of knucklehead

explanation.surface: Insults lined up: a clod, or a knucklehead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clod' sits right beside the definition and is a synonym itself, tempting as the definition, but it holds the start of the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dork and knucklehead are both informal insults for a stupid or socially awkward person.

clue.text: Cheese from France flipping scoffed

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to scoff is to eat greedily

explanation.surface: A French cheese, wolfed down in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads like a mild British swear word, but it signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a white brined Greek cheese, so it is an example of cheese.

clue.text: Prefer swallowing middle of Gentleman's Relish

indicators.note: swallowing means taking inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to prefer something is to favour it

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter

parts.note: the fifth of nine letters, the central one

explanation.surface: Choosing Gentleman's Relish, the British anchovy paste, by the mouthful.
explanation.walkthrough: Gentleman's Relish is a British anchovy spread, so the eye reads the brand name as one unit; the 's is a link meaning 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish as a noun means taste or savour, so flavour is a synonym.

clue.text: Currency problem leader's dismissed

indicators.note: with the leader sent away, the opening letter of the word goes

parts.note: a problem is a trouble

explanation.surface: A money crisis after the head of state is ousted.
explanation.definitionFit: The rouble is the currency of Russia, so it is an example of currency.

clue.text: Rising, adult put on perfume

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: A is the film classification for adult
perfume is a scent

explanation.surface: Getting up, a grown-up dabs on some fragrance.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is a climb or upward movement, matching the noun use of rising.

clue.text: Name bird with large tail in tree

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its very end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Identify a bird with a big tail perched in a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a long-tailed bird; 'tail' actually picks the last letter of tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A title is the name of a book, film or work, so it can stand for name.

clue.text: Responses from Republican before last of the lawsuits

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of what follows

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican

indicators.note: last of means just the final letter of the next word

parts.note: the final letter
a lawsuit is a legal action

explanation.surface: Political reactions from a Republican ahead of the final court cases.
explanation.definitionFit: Reactions are the ways people reply to an event, so they are responses.

clue.text: Rotates barrels in river? On the contrary

indicators.note: in on its own would put the barrels inside the river
on the contrary swaps the roles just stated, so the river goes inside the barrels instead

parts.note: a tun is a large cask
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Someone turning casks floating in a river, or the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the barrels would go inside the river; 'On the contrary' reverses that, putting river inside barrels.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn is to rotate, spin round on an axis; turns matches rotates as a present-tense verb.

clue.text: Forest worker runs by nettle

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
to nettle is to irritate, to anger

explanation.surface: A woodland employee hurries past a patch of stinging nettles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nettle' looks like the plant beside the path; it is the verb meaning irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: A forest ranger is employed to look after and patrol woodland.

clue.text: Her boiler, unfortunately losing energy, is awful

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome has gone wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order
to lose something is to be without it, so one letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Her boiler has broken down and lost power, which is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: One E is taken out of HER BOILER and the remaining eight letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Horrible and awful are close synonyms, both meaning very bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Newspapers the man found in stations

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: to station something is to set or place it, so stations means sets
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: A fellow spotted buying papers at railway stations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stations' looks like a noun for railway stops but is the verb meaning places or sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheets is informal for newspapers, especially downmarket ones, as in 'a scandal sheet'.

clue.text: Search for religious faction around Portugal

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the next

parts.note: a sect is a breakaway religious group
P is the international vehicle code for Portugal

explanation.surface: Hunting for a religious group operating around Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Search for' looks like the whole definition, but 'for' supplies PRO and only 'Search' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To prospect is to search an area for gold or minerals, so it is a kind of searching.
